description: FieldDynamics is building an adaptive decision-support tool combining AI and NASA Earth Observation data to solve the "Field Shift" challenge and empower farmers. We need: Software/Data Engineers: To scale backend & model satellite data. Web Devs/UI: To build an intuitive frontend.  Earth/Ag Scientists: To interpret climate data & ensure real-world value. Writers: To craft our pitch.
summary:
FieldDynamics (from FieldDynamics Lab) is a decision-support tool that helps extension advisors and smallholder farmers in Kaduna, Nigeria, explore crop rotation options. In a single farm visit, the advisor picks the local government area, records past crops and sets the farmer’s priorities, such as saving water or adding nitrogen to the soil. The tool then compares the current rotation with two alternatives and shows the evidence behind each.

It answers the Field Shift challenge by turning NASA Earth observations (POWER, SMAP, MODIS NDVI and GRACE-FO), together with CHIRPS rainfall and iSDA soil data, into local, explainable guidance. A transparent rule-based engine, with a water balance and stress-tested rankings, shows its confidence honestly. Results can be shared as WhatsApp text, a PNG, a print card or a radio script, and the interface works on phones in English and Hausa.

It matters because choosing the next crop is high-stakes when rains are shifting, and satellite data rarely reaches the field. FieldDynamics supports farmer judgment and local expertise, and never replaces them. 
(169 words)
details:
Who we are

Field Dynamics Labs is a registered NASA Space Apps team building a crop-rotation decision tool for extension advisers/smallholder farmers in Kaduna State, Nigeria. The team comprises:
1. Lenge Dandung Joshua, a data professional with a specialty in software engineering and data
2. Goodness Edet Mbakara, a software engineer and 7X hackathon winner
3. Maureen Obiekwe, a QA engineer with 6 years of experience carrying out the full Software Testing Lifecycle across fintech apps and other industries, covering payment flows, security, and users' usability of products without friction.

4. Deborah Anyachukwu, a biomedical engineer and software engineer.
5. Zahemen Bnejamin Anongo, specializing in Chemical and Petroleum Technology. I have experience in scientific research and data analysis.
6. Mohamed Agnaou, a chemical engineering student specializing in processes and formulation, with practical experience in environmental and analytical chemistry.

The project is not a new advice system. Kaduna already has advisors, weather forecasts, radio, and voice calls. Field Dynamics adds the missing piece, a crop-rotation layer powered by NASA data, to the systems that already exist. The advisor uses the tool on the phone they already carry, and the result reaches the farmer by WhatsApp, a printed card, or a radio script. Farmers install nothing. The tool supports the judgment of the advisor and the farmer; it does not replace it.

The problem


Rain-fed smallholders in northern Nigeria decide each year what to plant with little information. The region matters: BII reports that northern Nigeria produces 50 to 60 per cent of the country's maize. Yet advice rarely reaches farmers in person. The ideal extension ratio is one agent for 10 to 50 farmers, but in Nigeria it is closer to one agent for 10,000 farmers.

The advice that does reach farmers is mostly about timing. NiMet's 2026 outlook told Kaduna when rains were expected to start and stop, and warned of above-normal rainfall and flood risk. Nationally, NiMet also forecast erratic rainfall and prolonged dry spells. What farmers are not shown is which rotation fits their field, what it costs in water, and what could go wrong.

The rotation question matters because continuous maize degrades soil. A long-term trial at IAR Samaru (ABU Zaria) found that continuous maize left soil in low quality, while maize rotated with soybean or cowpea raised it to moderate quality. Farmers are told when to plant, but not what to plant next.

But Why Kaduna?

First, the rotation question is very real there. It’s in the northern Guinea savanna, part of Nigeria’s maize belt, where farmers rotate or intercrop maize with soybean, cowpea, and sorghum. That’s exactly the legume-cereal rotation story the brief describes.

Second, the climate pressure is visible: rain onset is shifting, dry spells are getting worse, and soils are degrading. It’s a transition zone. Kaduna sits between the wetter south and the drier north.

Third, and this is the big one, it has evidence. The Institute for Agricultural Research at Samaru in Zaria has run crop rotation trials for decades, which further backs up what we are trying to build. Also, Agritech is already active with more than 7 different tech solutions deployed; there’s an active extension network there. The state agricultural development programme has laid a real path to farmers, and Firms working across the North, like ThriveAgri, show farmers they can be reached digitally.

Already Existing Solutions
AGRA Kaduna Consortium with NAERLS (2021 to 2024): 1,082 CBAs (Community Based Advisors) trained; 677 subsidised smartphones; 281 CBAs trained on a farm-management app; processing centres in Zaria, Kubau, Makarfi.


NiMet Seasonal Climate Prediction, turned into the Kaduna State Farmers' Weather Guide 2025 by HEDA: Covers all 23 Kaduna LGAs; rain onset May 9 (Sanga) to June 10 (Makarfi); dry spell risk July 10 to 25

HarvestPlus Hausa radio service: Reported about 20 million farmers and women reached by the end of 2023 across 4 states, including Kaduna State.

Precision Development (PxD): Targeted 100,000+ farmers in 11 states; only 26% of surveyed farmers had other extension access

Crop2Cash: 20,701 farmers used the USSD service, including 5,627 women.

What FieldDynamics Does

FieldDynamics is a crop-rotation advisor for all 23 LGAs of Kaduna State, Nigeria. A farmer or extension officer gives the LGA what was planted in the last one or two seasons, soil, water access, equipment, where the crop is sold, up to three priorities, and the kind of season expected. FieldDynamics returns three cards: the farmer’s current rotation and the two best alternatives. Each card shows a score, a confidence level, and a plain reason for every line. Every number traces back to NASA and partner Earth observation data, and published field trials are used only to check the result.

How the product works

Reads 45 years of each LGA’s climate and land (1981 to 2025).

Rain: CHIRPS, with GPM IMERG for storm intensity.

Heat, humidity and evaporation: NASA POWER.

Soil moisture: SMAP and GLDAS.

Crop greenness: MODIS NDVI, cross-checked with VIIRS and Landsat/Sentinel-2 (HLS).

Slope: SRTM.

Surface temperature and evapotranspiration: MODIS.

Soil: iSDAsoil.

Farmland mask: ESA WorldCover.

Market prices: the Kaduna State Bureau of Statistics, 24 commodities across all 23 LGAs.

Sorts every season into one of four types using rain start, end, length, total, dry spells, and heat across 575 LGA-years: Wet (29%), Late start (25%), Typical (24%), Dry spell (22%). The farmer picks a type to see how each rotation holds up in that kind of year.

Runs an FAO-56 daily crop water balance for 9 crops in every LGA and year.

- Total rain is rarely the problem: crops get 2 to 3 times their water need.

- The real risk is timing. Maize finishes inside the rains in 99 to 100% of Typical and Wet years, but only 56% of Late-start years.

Scores every two-season rotation of 14 crops, including maize, sorghum, millet, soybean, cowpea, groundnut, sesame, rice, ginger, yam, cassava, tomato, lablab, and Stylosanthes.

- Filters: FAO ECOCROP climate and soil suitability for each LGA, plus the water and season-length rules.

- Scoring: up to seven lines: water, nitrogen, organic matter, erosion, pests and Striga, market, and animal feed.

- Weighting: each line is weighted by the LGA’s own need, and the farmer’s chosen priorities count three times.

Adds risk lines it never scores:

- humid spells that favour leaf blight in maize and sorghum;

- late dry spells before groundnut harvest, which raise aflatoxin risk;

- long-term trends: heat days are rising by about +11.7 per decade, significant in 16 of 23 LGAs, while rain start, season rain and dry spells show no significant change.

- Rates confidence High, Medium or Low for each LGA, based on how much farmland the LGA has, cloud gaps in the greenness record, and soil uncertainty.

How we know it works

- The data agrees with published trials it never saw. The rotations studied in published field trials from Nigeria and the wider West African savanna rank at the 83rd percentile of the engine’s own data-only ranking, against 47% for random rotations (p = 0.0001). Cereal-then-legume rotations rank between the 84th and 100th percentile.

- The season warning holds up on past years. Each LGA-year from 2000 to 2024 was predicted from the other years only. Warnings caught 85% of seasons where maize failed to finish inside the rains, with 10% false alarms, against 29% false alarms without the season type.

- We report what doesn’t work. Our crop-stress model could not beat the LGA’s own long-term normal, so the tool makes no crop-stress forecast. In three of the four worst greenness years, the rains were normal enough for maize to finish, so the cause lay outside water and timing. The tool says this on its Learn screen instead of claiming it would have flagged those years.

Benefits FieldDynamics Offers

For farmers: a clear, explained choice between what they plant now and the two best alternatives for their own LGA, instead of advice written for the whole state. Each line says why, such as “maize finishes inside the rains in only 56% of late-start years.”

For extension officers: one tool covers all 23 LGAs, gives an answer in under a second, and states its own confidence and what data it lacks.

For the soil and the season: it favours rotating cereals with legumes. Published trials show that adds 0.38 to 1.01 t/ha to the next maize crop and cuts Striga by 35 to 76%.

For trust: it says what it can’t do. Our crop-stress model had no skill, and the tool makes no claim about it.

Intended impact

Many Kaduna farmers plant maize after maize, which drains soil nitrogen, builds up Striga, and leaves them exposed to late or broken rains.

The aim: move rotation decisions from habit to evidence, one LGA and one season type at a time. That means fewer failed seasons, healthier soil, more legumes for food and animal feed, and income spread across more crops.

How it reaches farmers: through extension officers and farmer groups, a phone screen and shareable cards.

Beyond Kaduna: the same pipeline works for any region that open satellite data covers.

Tools, languages and software

Language: Python 3.12.

Data:

Google Earth Engine (aggregation runs on Google’s servers);

NASA POWER API and NASA Earthdata (earthaccess, h5py);

pandas, NumPy, xarray, rioxarray, GeoPandas.

Science and models:

SciPy, scikit-learn (K-means, Ridge);

LightGBM, with Optuna for tuning and SHAP for explanations;

pymannkendall for trends;

FAO-56 water balance and EcoCrop suitability, written by the team.

Pipeline: Jupyter notebooks run by nbclient, with every formula in tested modules.

App: FastAPI, Pydantic, Jinja2, Uvicorn, deployed on Vercel.

Quality:

- pytest (over 260 tests), Ruff and mypy;

- GitHub Actions CI, a security scan and preview deploys on every pull request;

- uv lock files with hashes for every installed package.

AI assistant: Claude (Anthropic), Argon (Gemini)

How it’s creative

Data leads, studies check. Most advisors start from expert recipes. Ours ranks every possible two-season rotation of 14 crops from data alone. Then it tests itself against published field trials it never saw: those rotations land at the 83rd percentile against 47% for random ones (p = 0.0001).

Four season types learned from 45 years of satellite data become a selector. The farmer sees how a rotation holds up in a wet, late-start, typical, or dry-spell year.

Risk is separate from score. Humid spells that favour leaf blight and dry spells before groundnut harvest (aflatoxin risk) appear as warnings, never as hidden penalties.

Every card carries a confidence level and a list of missing data. A model that failed is reported as failed.

Factors considered

Cost:

- Only free, open data.

- Earth Engine reduces the satellite data to small LGA tables on Google’s servers, so we never download raw rasters.

- The live app reads a 150 KB data bundle and runs serverless on a free-tier host.

Energy

- All heavy computation runs once, offline.

- The live app only scores, in about 40 ms, with no GPU.

- Maps and outputs are precomputed.

Accessibility:

- Designed for phones first: tap-friendly controls, visible labels and readable contrast.

- Plain language, a Hausa version planned, and cards that can be shared or printed.

Data limits:

- Low-farmland and city LGAs are flagged as lower confidence.

- Satellite products are cross-checked against each other. NASA POWER rainfall was dropped after it failed our checks (single days over 1,000 mm).

Privacy and security: secrets stay out of the code, every change passes a security gate, and users can delete their data.

Use of AI-generated code

  • Who did what: the team used Claude as a coding and research assistant. We defined the problem, the questions and every key decision, including “data leads, studies only check” and dropping a model with no skill. Claude helped write pipeline code, tests and documentation, and searched the literature.
    • small pull requests, each reviewed by a person;
    • automated tests with known answers (FAO-56 worked examples);
    • CI on a clean machine, and a security scan.
    • an assistant-written engine that only worked with local files failed in CI and was fixed before merge;
    • leakage tests stopped an over-optimistic model score from being claimed.

Accountable for every number: each figure traces to a script, a dataset and a logged experiment (docs/experiments.csv), and the team can explain every one.
